title: His own compositions and publishing income from overseas
summary: He wrote instrumentals named as inside jokes; except for Skyliner, most royalty income from his two publishing companies now comes from overseas.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: All right. You've written some tunes. When did you start writing?

Well, I think most musicians at some time or another fancy themselves as being some kind of a song writer. I wrote instrumental tunes, you know, tunes that I was thinking of how the band would sound. I wasn't thinking of -- oh, there may have been a couple that had lyrics that were aimed both ways, but basically I was thinking instrumentally. As far as the names are concerned, they don't make much sense. A lot of them, you know, they're named after something that happened, and -- or after -- they're inside jokes, a lot of them. As was the case with most of the instrumentals that were played by bands. Outside of, "Skyliner," "Skyliner," of course, has been an important copyright, but the rest of them -- well, we get some performances, mostly overseas now. But not in the United States. It's a strange thing. It used to be that 10 percent of your income from that category would come from overseas and 90 percent from the United States. I have these two music publishing companies, it's just the opposite now. 90 percent comes from overseas, and by overseas I mean both directions, Japan, Australia, Europe, you name it, and practically nothing from here.
